title: Circular Polarization
short_intro: Circular polarization is a state of optical polarization where the electric field vector of a light wave maintains a constant magnitude while continuously rotating in a plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation at an optical frequency. It is produced by the superposition of two orthogonal, phase-quadrature linear polarizations of equal amplitude.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of circularly polarized light, conditions for production using quarter-wave plates, and qualitative distinction between linear, circular, and elliptical polarization.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical description of Jones vectors for circular polarization, phase difference condition (pi/2 or odd multiples), optical rotation, handedness (left-circular and right-circular), and birefringence in uniaxial crystals.

prerequisites: Superposition principle of orthogonal harmonic oscillations
Double refraction and uniaxial crystals (ordinary and extraordinary rays)

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Wave Characteristics
bullets: The electric field vector traces out a circle as a function of time at a given point in space, or as a function of position at a given instant.
The tip of the electric field vector rotates with an angular frequency equal to the angular frequency of the light wave, omega.
The magnitude of the electric field remains constant: E<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> + E<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> = E<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Production
bullets: Two mutually orthogonal linear polarization components (E<sub>x</sub> and E<sub>y</sub>) must have equal amplitudes.
There must be a constant phase difference of delta = (2n + 1)π/2 between the two orthogonal components, where n is an integer.
Typically achieved by passing plane-polarized light through a quarter-wave plate with its optic axis oriented at 45 degrees to the incident polarization azimuth.

concept_notes.heading: Handedness (Right- and Left-Circular Polarization)
bullets: Right-Circularly Polarized (RCP) light corresponds to a clockwise rotation of the electric vector when viewed facing the oncoming wave.
Left-Circularly Polarized (LCP) light corresponds to a counter-clockwise rotation of the electric vector when viewed facing the oncoming wave.
In IEEE convention, RCP is designated by a phase delay of E<sub>y</sub> relative to E<sub>x</sub> by +π/2.

concept_notes.heading: Detection and Analysis
bullets: Circularly polarized light cannot be distinguished from unpolarized light using a single rotating polarizer alone, as the transmitted intensity remains constant.
A quarter-wave plate is used to convert circularly polarized light back into linearly polarized light, which can then be completely extinguished by an analyzer.
Combination of a quarter-wave plate and a linear analyzer uniquely identifies circular polarization.

derivations.title: Mathematical Derivation of Circular Polarization
derivations.conditions: Two orthogonal linear waves of equal amplitude E<sub>0</sub> and a phase difference of π/2
steps: Write the x-component of the electric field: E_x(z, t) = E_0 \cos(\omega t - kz)
Write the y-component with a phase lead of π/2: E_y(z, t) = E_0 \cos(\omega t - kz + \frac{\pi}{2}) = -E_0 \sin(\omega t - kz)
Square both components and add them: E_x^2 + E_y^2 = E_0^2 \cos^2(\omega t - kz) + E_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t - kz) = E_0^2
derivations.result: E_x^2 + E_y^2 = E_0^2, which represents the equation of a circle in the xy-plane.

derivations.title: Action of a Quarter-Wave Plate
derivations.conditions: Incident linearly polarized light at 45 degrees to the optic axis of a negative uniaxial crystal
steps: Resolve incident amplitude E<sub>0</sub> into components parallel (E<sub>||</sub>) and perpendicular (E<sub>⊥</sub>) to the optic axis: E_x = E_0 \cos(45^\circ) and E_y = E_0 \sin(45^\circ)
Introduce a phase difference Δφ = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(n_e - n_o)d = \frac{\pi}{2} due to the thickness d of the quarter-wave plate
The emergent orthogonal components have equal amplitude and a π/2 phase difference, satisfying the circular polarization condition.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Helical trajectory of electric vector
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A 3D coordinate system (x, y, z) showing a corkscrew-like helical path of the tip of the E vector winding around the propagation axis z.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how the magnitude of E remains constant while its direction rotates uniformly in planes perpendicular to z.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in conceptual questions identifying polarization states from spatial field profiles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Production using a Linear Polarizer and Quarter-Wave Plate
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Unpolarized light source -> Linear Polarizer (transmission axis at 45°) -> Quarter-Wave Plate (optic axis horizontal) -> Circularly polarized beam.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the optical components required to transform unpolarized light into circularly polarized light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in experimental setup identification for TGT and PGT.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Analyzer rotation test
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of transmitted intensity I versus rotation angle θ of a linear analyzer showing a flat straight line (I = constant).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that circularly polarized light shows no intensity variation upon rotating a single analyzer.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing circular polarization from partial or complete linear polarization.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the minimum thickness of a quarter-wave plate for light of wavelength 589 nm, given that the ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices are n_o = 1.544 and n_e = 1.553.
solution_steps: Identify given values: λ = 589 nm = 589 \times 10^{-9} m, n_o = 1.544, n_e = 1.553
Use the quarter-wave plate thickness formula: d = \frac{\lambda}{4(n_e - n_o)}

solved_numericals.question: The electric field of a monochromatic light wave is given by \vec{E} = E_0 [\hat{i} \cos(\omega t - kz) - \hat{j} \sin(\omega t - kz)]. Determine the state of polarization and its handedness.
solution_steps: Identify components: E_x = E_0 \cos(\omega t - kz) and E_y = -E_0 \sin(\omega t - kz)
Check amplitudes: Both components have equal amplitude E_0.
Check phase relationship: E_y can be written as E_0 \cos(\omega t - kz + \pi/2), meaning E_y leads E_x by π/2.
Determine rotation direction: At z = 0, at t = 0, E = E_0 \hat{i}. At \omega t = \pi/2, E = -E_0 \hat{j}. The vector rotates clockwise when facing the source.

solved_numericals.question: A beam of circularly polarized light of intensity I_0 is incident normally on a rotating linear polarizer. What is the intensity of the transmitted light as a function of time, and what is its average value?
solution_steps: Circularly polarized light has an electric field vector of constant magnitude E_0 rotating at angular frequency ω.
When passing through a linear polarizer, only the component parallel to the transmission axis is transmitted: E(t) = E_0 \cos(\omega t).
Transmitted intensity is proportional to the square of the electric field: I(t) = I_0 \cos^2(\omega t), where I_0 is the maximum intensity.
Take the time average over one complete cycle: \langle \cos^2(\omega t) \rangle = 1/2.
solved_numericals.answer: I(t) = I_0 \cos^2(\omega t) with a time-averaged intensity of I_0 / 2

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes monochromatic light waves of stable frequency and well-defined phase.
Birefringent crystals are treated as homogeneous and uniaxial with fixed principal refractive indices.
Multiple internal reflections within the wave plate are neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Circularly polarized light can be identified by passing it through a single rotating polarizer and observing extinction.
common_misconceptions.correct: A single rotating polarizer yields constant intensity for both unpolarized and circularly polarized light.
common_misconceptions.why: A single polarizer cannot introduce the phase retardation needed to analyze circular polarization; a quarter-wave plate must precede the polarizer.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The magnitude of the electric field vector changes as it rotates in circular polarization.
common_misconceptions.correct: The magnitude of the electric field vector remains strictly constant in circular polarization.
common_misconceptions.why: A constant magnitude with a continuously changing direction defines the circle in the transverse plane; varying magnitude results in elliptical polarization.

quick_revision: Circular polarization requires two orthogonal linear components of equal amplitude and a π/2 phase difference.
A quarter-wave plate introduces a π/2 phase shift to convert linear polarization to circular polarization.
The intensity of circularly polarized light does not change upon rotating a single linear analyzer.
